claim: The supramammillary nucleus (SuM) provides substantial innervation to the dentate gyrus (DG).
source: The supramammillary nucleus (SuM) provides substantial innervation to the dentate gyrus (DG).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established fact about anatomical connectivity.

claim: SuM-DG Ca2+ activities are highly correlated during spatial memory retrieval as compared to the moderate correlation during memory encoding when mice are performing a location discrimination task.
source: Here we report that SuM-DG Ca2+ activities are highly correlated during spatial memory retrieval as compared to the moderate correlation during memory encoding when mice are performing a location discrimination task.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo multi-fiber photometry recordings presented in Figure 1 showing correlation coefficients during different memory phases.

claim: The activity of SuM neurons is required for spatial memory retrieval.
source: Supporting this evidence, we demonstrate that the activity of SuM neurons or SuM-DG projections is required for spatial memory retrieval.
evidence: This is supported by chemogenetic and optogenetic manipulation experiments shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: The activity of SuM-DG projections is required for spatial memory retrieval.
source: Supporting this evidence, we demonstrate that the activity of SuM neurons or SuM-DG projections is required for spatial memory retrieval.
evidence: This is supported by optogenetic manipulation experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: SuM glutamate transmission is necessary for spatial memory retrieval.
source: Furthermore, we show that SuM glutamate transmission is necessary for both spatial memory retrieval and highly-correlated SuM-DG activities during spatial memory retrieval.
evidence: This is supported by genetic knockdown experiments shown in Figures 4, 5, and 6.

claim: SuM glutamate transmission is necessary for highly-correlated SuM-DG activities during spatial memory retrieval.
source: Furthermore, we show that SuM glutamate transmission is necessary for both spatial memory retrieval and highly-correlated SuM-DG activities during spatial memory retrieval.
evidence: This is supported by photometry recordings in shVglut2 mice shown in Figure 6.

claim: The dentate gyrus (DG) is the first input region of the hippocampus.
source: The dentate gyrus (DG) is the first input region of the hippocampus, in which DG granule cells (GCs) receive major excitatory inputs from the entorhinal cortex (EC) and send excitatory outputs to CA3 through mossy fibers (Bao and Song, 2018; Knierim and Neunuebel, 2016; Treves et al., 2008; Vivar and van Praag, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: DG granule cells (GCs) receive major excitatory inputs from the entorhinal cortex (EC).
source: The dentate gyrus (DG) is the first input region of the hippocampus, in which DG granule cells (GCs) receive major excitatory inputs from the entorhinal cortex (EC) and send excitatory outputs to CA3 through mossy fibers (Bao and Song, 2018; Knierim and Neunuebel, 2016; Treves et al., 2008; Vivar and van Praag, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: DG granule cells send excitatory outputs to CA3 through mossy fibers.
source: The dentate gyrus (DG) is the first input region of the hippocampus, in which DG granule cells (GCs) receive major excitatory inputs from the entorhinal cortex (EC) and send excitatory outputs to CA3 through mossy fibers (Bao and Song, 2018; Knierim and Neunuebel, 2016; Treves et al., 2008; Vivar and van Praag, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: GCs are the principal neurons in the DG that exhibit sparse firing.
source: GCs are the principal neurons in the DG that exhibit sparse firing, thus establishing sparse GC-CA3 connectivity to contribute to spatial information processing (Knierim and Neunuebel, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: Sparse GC-CA3 connectivity contributes to spatial information processing.
source: GCs are the principal neurons in the DG that exhibit sparse firing, thus establishing sparse GC-CA3 connectivity to contribute to spatial information processing (Knierim and Neunuebel, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: The DG receives inputs from subcortical regions, such as the medial septum and the supramammillary nucleus (SuM) of the hypothalamus.
source: Besides the major cortical inputs from EC, the DG also receives inputs from subcortical regions, such as the medial septum and the supramammillary nucleus (SuM) of the hypothalamus (Leranth and Hajszan, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: Subcortical regions play critical roles in regulating hippocampal theta rhythm.
source: It has been well established that these subcortical regions play critical roles in regulating hippocampal theta rhythm, which is widely known to be important for spatial information processing (Kocsis and Vertes, 1997; Pan and McNaughton, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Hippocampal theta rhythm is important for spatial information processing.
source: It has been well established that these subcortical regions play critical roles in regulating hippocampal theta rhythm, which is widely known to be important for spatial information processing (Kocsis and Vertes, 1997; Pan and McNaughton, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: SuM sends dense projections to DG GCs.
source: In this study, we focus on the SuM inputs to the DG, based on the dense projections from SuM to DG GCs (Berger et al., 2001; Pedersen et al., 2017; Soussi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Both SuM and DG have been implicated in hippocampal-dependent spatial memory.
source: Both SuM and DG have been implicated in hippocampal-dependent spatial memory (Ito et al., 2018; Vertes, 2015), but how SuM and DG coordinate their activities during distinct stages of the memory process and ultimately regulate this process is unknown.
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: SuM-DG axonal terminals co-release glutamate and GABA to the DG.
source: Furthermore, recent studies demonstrated that SuM-DG axonal terminals co-release glutamate and GABA to the DG (Hashimotodani et al., 2018; Root et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: The Ca2+ events from the SuM and DG neurons are correlated in the range of 0.1–0.5 Hz.
source: Correlation analysis based on frequency spectrums showed that the Ca2+ events from the SuM and DG neurons are correlated in the range of 0.1–0.5 Hz (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–I).
evidence: This is supported by spectral analysis data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The Ca2+ events from SuM and DG were moderately correlated (R = 0.4, p<0.001) at baseline when mice were placed at their home cages.
source: Therefore, we extracted the Ca2+ signals from this frequency range, and found that the Ca2+ events from these two brain regions were moderately correlated (R = 0.4, p<0.001) at baseline when mice were placed at their home cages (Figure 1D–E).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis data shown in Figure 1D-E.

claim: During spatial memory encoding (familiarization phase), mice spent equal amount of time exploring both objects.
source: Consistent with previous reports (Sawangjit et al., 2018), we found that during spatial memory encoding (familiarization phase), mice spent equal amount of time exploring both objects; while during spatial memory retrieval (test phase), mice spent significantly more time exploring the object associated with the new location than that associated with the old location (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1G and citation to previous work.

claim: During spatial memory retrieval (test phase), mice spent significantly more time exploring the object associated with the new location than that associated with the old location.
source: Consistent with previous reports (Sawangjit et al., 2018), we found that during spatial memory encoding (familiarization phase), mice spent equal amount of time exploring both objects; while during spatial memory retrieval (test phase), mice spent significantly more time exploring the object associated with the new location than that associated with the old location (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1G and citation to previous work.

claim: During memory encoding, Ca2+ activities in the SuM and DG were moderately increased from the baseline.
source: Interestingly, during memory encoding, when mice were investigating objects at their relative locations, Ca2+ activities in the SuM and DG were moderately increased from the baseline (Figure 1H–J) and were moderately correlated (Figure 1K, R = 0.54, p = 0.01).
evidence: This is supported by photometry data shown in Figure 1H-J.

claim: During memory encoding, Ca2+ activities in the SuM and DG were moderately correlated (R = 0.54, p = 0.01).
source: Interestingly, during memory encoding, when mice were investigating objects at their relative locations, Ca2+ activities in the SuM and DG were moderately increased from the baseline (Figure 1H–J) and were moderately correlated (Figure 1K, R = 0.54, p = 0.01).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 1K.

claim: During spatial memory retrieval, the Ca2+ activities in the SuM and DG were significantly increased from the baseline.
source: Strikingly, during spatial memory retrieval when mice were trying to recall the objects/locations, the Ca2+ activities in the SuM and DG were significantly increased from the baseline (Figure 1L–N), and Ca2+ events were highly correlated (Figure 1O, R = 0.92, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is supported by photometry data shown in Figure 1L-N.

claim: During spatial memory retrieval, Ca2+ events in the SuM and DG were highly correlated (R = 0.92, p<0.0001).
source: Strikingly, during spatial memory retrieval when mice were trying to recall the objects/locations, the Ca2+ activities in the SuM and DG were significantly increased from the baseline (Figure 1L–N), and Ca2+ events were highly correlated (Figure 1O, R = 0.92, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 1O.

claim: Ca2+ activities in the SuM and DG were significantly higher during memory retrieval than encoding.
source: While Ca2+ activities in the SuM and DG were increased during both spatial memory encoding and retrieval, they were significantly higher in both SuM and DG during memory retrieval than encoding (Figure 1P–Q).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 1P-Q.

claim: EC and DG Ca2+ activities exhibit low correlation (R = 0.22, p > 0.05) when mice were at their home cage.
source: Interestingly, despite that EC and DG are highly connected anatomically, their Ca2+ activities exhibit low correlation when mice were at their home cage (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C–D, R = 0.22, p > 0.05).
evidence: This is supported by photometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C-D.

claim: Both the DG and EC activities were increased during spatial memory retrieval in the NPR test.
source: Importantly, although both the DG and EC activities were increased during spatial memory retrieval in the NPR test, the correlation of their Ca2+ activities was not significantly altered (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E–H, R = 0.21, p>0.05).
evidence: This is supported by photometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2E-H.

claim: The correlation of DG and EC Ca2+ activities was not significantly altered during spatial memory retrieval (R = 0.21, p>0.05).
source: Importantly, although both the DG and EC activities were increased during spatial memory retrieval in the NPR test, the correlation of their Ca2+ activities was not significantly altered (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E–H, R = 0.21, p>0.05).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2E-H.

claim: There are two distinct pathways from the SuM to DG with distinct neurotransmitter systems.
source: It has been suggested that there are two distinct pathways from the SuM to DG with distinct neurotransmitter systems. One pathway originates from the lateral SuM (SuML) expressing markers for both GABA (Vgat: vesicular GABA transporter) and glutamate (Vglut2: vesicular glutamate transporter 2) (Pedersen et al., 2017; Soussi et al., 2010). The other pathway originates from the medial SuM (SuMM) mainly expressing VGLUT2 (Vertes, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: One pathway originates from the lateral SuM (SuML) expressing markers for both GABA (Vgat) and glutamate (Vglut2).
source: One pathway originates from the lateral SuM (SuML) expressing markers for both GABA (Vgat: vesicular GABA transporter) and glutamate (Vglut2: vesicular glutamate transporter 2) (Pedersen et al., 2017; Soussi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: The other pathway originates from the medial SuM (SuMM) mainly expressing VGLUT2.
source: The other pathway originates from the medial SuM (SuMM) mainly expressing VGLUT2 (Vertes, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: Major inputs from SuM to DG GCs are located in the SuML.
source: Specifically, our rabies tracing revealed that major inputs from SuM to DG GCs are located in the SuML (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-E), and nearly 80% of DG-projecting SuML neurons are positive for GABA (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F-G).
evidence: This is supported by rabies tracing data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-E.

claim: Nearly 80% of DG-projecting SuML neurons are positive for GABA.
source: Specifically, our rabies tracing revealed that major inputs from SuM to DG GCs are located in the SuML (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-E), and nearly 80% of DG-projecting SuML neurons are positive for GABA (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F-G).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F-G.

claim: SuMLVgat neurons send dense projections to the granule cell layer of the DG.
source: Supporting the retrograde tracing data, our anterograde tracing of SuML Vgat+ (SuMLVgat) neurons confirmed that SuMLVgat neurons send dense projections to the granule cell layer of the DG (Figure 2—figure supplement 1H-J).
evidence: This is supported by anterograde tracing data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1H-J.

claim: Activation of SuMLVgat neurons increases the density of c-Fos+ GCs.
source: Interestingly, we found that activation or inhibition of SuMLVgat neurons increases or decreases the density of c-Fos+ GCs, respectively (Figure 2B–E).
evidence: This is supported by c-Fos immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2B-E.

claim: Inhibition of SuMLVgat neurons decreases the density of c-Fos+ GCs.
source: Interestingly, we found that activation or inhibition of SuMLVgat neurons increases or decreases the density of c-Fos+ GCs, respectively (Figure 2B–E).
evidence: This is supported by c-Fos immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2B-E.

claim: Chemogenetic activation of SuML neurons increases Ca2+ activity in DG GCs.
source: Consistent with increased density of cFos+ GCs, we found increased Ca2+ activity in DG GCs upon chemogenetic activation of SuML neurons (Figure 2G–I).
evidence: This is supported by photometry data shown in Figure 2G-I.

claim: The SuMLVgat activity is required for modulating GC activity through the excitatory glutamate component.
source: These results suggest that the SuMLVgat activity is required for modulating GC activity through the excitatory glutamate component.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the c-Fos and photometry data showing increased GC activity upon SuML activation.

claim: Activation of SuMLVgat neurons increased the discrimination ratio in the NPR test.
source: Interestingly, we found that activation or inhibition of SuMLVgat neurons increased or decreased the discrimination ratio in the hippocampus-dependent NPR test, respectively (Figure 2K).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2K.

claim: Inhibition of SuMLVgat neurons decreased the discrimination ratio in the NPR test.
source: Interestingly, we found that activation or inhibition of SuMLVgat neurons increased or decreased the discrimination ratio in the hippocampus-dependent NPR test, respectively (Figure 2K).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2K.

claim: Activation or inhibition of SuMLVgat neurons did not affect the discrimination ratio in the novel-object recognition (NOR) test.
source: In contrast, activation or inhibition of SuMLVgat neurons did not affect the discrimination ratio in the novel-object recognition (NOR) test, which is a non-spatial memory test (Cohen et al., 2013; Oliveira et al., 2010; Sawangjit et al., 2018; Winters et al., 2004; Winters et al., 2008; Figure 2L).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2L and citations to literature establishing NOR as a non-spatial memory test.

claim: CNO administration did not alter the locomotor activity of the mice in the open field test.
source: Importantly, CNO administration did not alter the locomotor activity of the mice in the open field test (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A-D) or average running speed of the mice during the NPR test (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E-F).
evidence: This is supported by locomotor activity data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A-D.

claim: CNO administration did not alter the average running speed of the mice during the NPR test.
source: Importantly, CNO administration did not alter the locomotor activity of the mice in the open field test (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A-D) or average running speed of the mice during the NPR test (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E-F).
evidence: This is supported by running speed data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2E-F.

claim: Chemogenetic activation of SuMM neurons does not significantly increase the discrimination ratio in the NPR test.
source: As a result, we found that chemogenetic activation of SuMM neurons does not significantly increase the discrimination ratio in the NPR test (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3C.

claim: SuML neurons, but not SuMM neurons, regulate spatial memory retrieval during the NPR test.
source: These results indicate that SuML neurons, but not SuMM neurons, regulate spatial memory retrieval during the NPR test.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the differential effects of SuML vs SuMM activation on NPR performance.

claim: Optogenetic activation of the SuMLVgat-DG projections induced both glutamatergic excitatory postsynaptic currents (oEPSCs) and GABAergic inhibitory postsynaptic currents (oIPSCs) in 70.6% of recorded cells.
source: Importantly, optogenetic activation of the SuMLVgat-DG projections induced both glutamatergic excitatory postsynaptic currents (oEPSCs, holding at −60 mV) and GABAergic inhibitory postsynaptic currents (oIPSCs, holding at +5 mV) in 70.6% of recorded cells (Figure 3C–D).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3C-D.

claim: The mean amplitude of oEPSCs is significantly higher than oIPSCs.
source: Interestingly, we found that the mean amplitude of oEPSCs is significantly higher than oIPSCs (Figure 3E–F).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3E-F.

claim: 17.8% of recorded cells exhibited solo oEPSCs, and no recorded cells exhibited solo oIPSCs.
source: In addition, 17.8% of recorded cells exhibited solo oEPSCs, and no recorded cells exhibited solo oIPSCs (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Optogenetic activation of SuMLVgat-DG projections increases the density of cFos+ GCs in vivo.
source: Supporting this notion, we found a significant increase in the density of cFos+ GCs upon optogenetic activation of SuMLVgat-DG projections in vivo (Figure 3H–J).
evidence: This is supported by c-Fos immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3H-J.

claim: Optogenetic activation of SuMLVgat-DG projections specifically during spatial memory encoding had no significant effects on the discrimination ratio of the mice in the NPR test.
source: Furthermore, optogenetic activation of SuMLVgat-DG projections specifically during spatial memory encoding had no significant effects on the discrimination ratio of the mice in the NPR test (Figure 3K).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3K.

claim: Optogenetic activation of SuMLVgat-DG projections specifically during spatial memory retrieval significantly increased the discrimination ratio of the mice in the NPR test.
source: In contrast, optogenetic activation of SuMLVgat-DG projections specifically during spatial memory retrieval significantly increased the discrimination ratio of the mice in the NPR test (Figure 3L).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3L.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of SuMLVgat-DG projections did not significantly alter the running speed of the mice.
source: As a control parameter, we measured the running speed of the mice during optogenetic stimulation of SuMLVgat-DG projections, and did not find significant alterations (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G–H), suggesting that the general activity of the mice does not contribute to the increased discrimination ratio observed in the NPR test.
evidence: This is supported by running speed data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1G-H.

claim: Optogenetic inhibition of SuMLVgat-DG projections during memory retrieval significantly decreased the discrimination ratio in the NPR test.
source: As a result, we found that optogenetic inhibition of SuMLVgat-DG projections during memory retrieval significantly decreased the discrimination ratio in the NPR test (Figure 3N).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3N.

claim: Optogenetic inhibition of SuMLVgat-DG projections during memory encoding did not alter the discrimination ratio.
source: In contrast, optogenetic inhibition of SuMLVgat-DG projections during memory encoding did not alter the discrimination ratio (Figure 3M–N).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3M-N.

claim: The activity of the SuML-DG circuit during the spatial memory retrieval (but not encoding) phase is both sufficient and necessary for regulating spatial memory performance.
source: Together, these results suggest that the activity of the SuML-DG circuit during the spatial memory retrieval (but not encoding) phase is both sufficient and necessary for regulating spatial memory performance.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the optogenetic activation and inhibition experiments during different memory phases.

claim: Optogenetic activation of SuMLVgat-CA2 projections did not significantly alter the discrimination ratio in the NPR test.
source: As a result, we found that optogenetic activation of SuMLVgat-CA2 projections did not significantly alter the discrimination ratio in the NPR test (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), indicating that SuMLVgat-CA2 projections are not sufficient to regulate spatial memory retrieval during the NPR test.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: SuMLVgat-CA2 projections are not sufficient to regulate spatial memory retrieval during the NPR test.
source: As a result, we found that optogenetic activation of SuMLVgat-CA2 projections did not significantly alter the discrimination ratio in the NPR test (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), indicating that SuMLVgat-CA2 projections are not sufficient to regulate spatial memory retrieval during the NPR test.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the lack of effect of SuMLVgat-CA2 activation on NPR performance.

claim: Knocking down Vglut2 in SuML neurons led to reduced Vglut2+ SuML-DG terminals.
source: Specifically, our immunohistology using antibodies against Vglut2 or Vgat demonstrated reduced Vglut2+ or Vgat+ SuML-DG terminals in shVglut2 or shVgat mice, respectively, as compared to those in the control mice injected with control AAVs for shVglut2 or shVgat (shControl mice) (Figure 4B,D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Knocking down Vgat in SuML neurons led to reduced Vgat+ SuML-DG terminals.
source: Specifically, our immunohistology using antibodies against Vglut2 or Vgat demonstrated reduced Vglut2+ or Vgat+ SuML-DG terminals in shVglut2 or shVgat mice, respectively, as compared to those in the control mice injected with control AAVs for shVglut2 or shVgat (shControl mice) (Figure 4B,D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Slice recordings of the GCs in shVglut2 injected mice showed a significant decrease only in the mean amplitude of oEPSCs, but not oIPSC.
source: Our slice recordings of the GCs in shVglut2 injected mice showed a significant decrease only in the mean amplitude of oEPSCs, but not oIPSC, respectively (Figure 4F–G).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4F-G.

claim: The latency of oIPSCs or oEPSCs in shVgat and shVglut2 mice was not significantly different from the shControl mice.
source: The latency of oIPSCs or oEPSCs in shVgat and shVglut2 mice was not significantly different from the shControl mice (Figure 4H–I), suggesting that knocking down glutamate component does not alter the nature of monosynaptic connections between SuMLVgat neurons and DG GCs.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4H-I.

claim: Knocking down the glutamate component in SuML neurons led to 38% of GCs exhibiting solo oIPSCs in shVglut2 mice, as compared to the control mice with no GCs having solo oIPSCs.
source: Strikingly, knocking down the glutamate component in SuML neurons led to 38% of GCs exhibiting solo oIPSCs in shVglut2 mice, as compared to the control mice with no GCs having solo oIPSCs (Figure 4J), suggesting that reducing glutamate release from SuML neurons may exert more inhibition on DG GCs.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4J.

claim: There was a decreased density of c-Fos+ GCs in shVglut2 mice after optogenetic activation of the SuML-DG projections.
source: Supporting this, we found a decreased density of c-Fos+ GCs in shVglut2 mice after optogenetic activation of the SuML-DG projections (Figure 4K–L).
evidence: This is supported by c-Fos immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4K-L.

claim: Knocking down the GABA component in SuML neurons led to a significant reduction in the mean amplitude of oIPSCs upon optogenetic stimulation of SuMLVgat-DG projections.
source: In contrast, knocking down the GABA component in SuML neurons led to a significant reduction in the mean amplitude of oIPSCs upon optogenetic stimulation of SuMLVgat-DG projections (Figure 4G), but did not alter the distribution of GCs exhibiting solo oEPSCs or dual oEPSCs and oIPSCs (Figure 4J).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Knocking down the GABA component in SuML neurons did not alter the distribution of GCs exhibiting solo oEPSCs or dual oEPSCs and oIPSCs.
source: In contrast, knocking down the GABA component in SuML neurons led to a significant reduction in the mean amplitude of oIPSCs upon optogenetic stimulation of SuMLVgat-DG projections (Figure 4G), but did not alter the distribution of GCs exhibiting solo oEPSCs or dual oEPSCs and oIPSCs (Figure 4J).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4J.

claim: The density of c-Fos+ GCs in shVgat mice after optogenetic activation of the SuML-DG projections did not significantly change as compared to shControl mice.
source: The density of c-Fos+ GCs in shVgat mice after optogenetic activation of the SuML-DG projections did not significantly change as compared to shControl mice (Figure 4K–L).
evidence: This is supported by c-Fos immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4K-L.

claim: Knocking down the glutamate component in SuML has a more profound effect on GC activity than knocking down the GABA component.
source: Based on these results, it appeared that knocking down the glutamate component in SuML has a more profound effect on GC activity than knocking down the GABA component.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the differential effects of shVglut2 vs shVgat on GC activity measures.

claim: shVglut2 (but not shVgat) mice exhibited a significant decrease in the discrimination ratio in the NPR test.
source: We found that shVglut2 (but not shVgat) mice, exhibited a significant decrease in the discrimination ratio in the NPR test (Figure 5B–C).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 5B-C.

claim: No significant change in the discrimination ratio in the NOR test was found in both shVglut2 and shVgat mice.
source: In contrast, we found no significant change in the discrimination ratio in the NOR test in both shVglut2 and shVgat mice (Figure 5D-E).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 5D-E.

claim: Glutamate transmission from SuML neurons is required for hippocampal-dependent spatial memory retrieval.
source: These results suggest that glutamate transmission from SuML neurons is required for hippocampal-dependent spatial memory retrieval.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the selective impairment of NPR (but not NOR) performance in shVglut2 mice.

claim: shVglut2 (but not shVgat) mice exhibit a significant reduction of the discrimination ratio upon optogenetic stimulation of SuMLVgat-DG projections during the NPR test.
source: Similarly, we found that shVglut2 (but not shVgat) mice exhibit a significant reduction of the discrimination ratio (Figure 5G–H).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 5G-H.

claim: Knocking down shVglut2 did not alter the DG and SuML activity in their home cage.
source: Interestingly, knocking down shVglut2 did not alter the DG and SuML activity in their home cage (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by photometry data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: shVglut2 mice exhibited a significant reduction in the correlation of the Ca2+ activities between SuM and DG at home cage as compared to the control mice.
source: However, shVglut2 mice exhibited a significant reduction in the correlation of the Ca2+ activities between SuM and DG as compared to the control mice (Figure 6D–F).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 6D-F.

claim: shVglut2 mice exhibited significantly reduced DG Ca2+ activity during spatial memory retrieval in the NPR test.
source: Furthermore, shVglut2 mice exhibited significantly reduced DG Ca2+ activity during spatial memory retrieval in the NPR test (Figure 6G–I).
evidence: This is supported by photometry data shown in Figure 6G-I.

claim: No significant alteration in the SuM Ca2+ activity was observed in shVglut2 mice during spatial memory retrieval.
source: In contrast, no significant alteration in the SuM Ca2+ activity was observed in shVglut2 mice during spatial memory retrieval (Figure 6I).
evidence: This is supported by photometry data shown in Figure 6I.

claim: SuML glutamate transmission is necessary for regulating the activity level of the DG during spatial memory retrieval.
source: These data suggest that SuML glutamate transmission is necessary for regulating the activity level of the DG during spatial memory retrieval.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the reduced DG activity in shVglut2 mice during memory retrieval.

claim: A significant reduction in the correlation of Ca2+ activities between the SuM and DG was found in shVglut2 mice during spatial memory retrieval during the NPR test.
source: Moreover, we measured the correlation of SuM and DG activities during spatial memory retrieval during the NPR test and found a significant reduction in the correlation of Ca2+ activities between the SuM and DG in shVglut2 mice (Figure 6J).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 6J.

claim: SuML glutamate release is necessary for regulating the DG activity and establishing the high correlation of the activities between SuM and DG during spatial memory retrieval.
source: Together, these results indicate that SuML glutamate release is necessary for regulating the DG activity and establishing the high correlation of the activities between SuM and DG during spatial memory retrieval.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the reduced DG activity and SuM-DG correlation in shVglut2 mice during memory retrieval.

claim: Activities of SuM and DG become significantly higher and correlated during spatial memory retrieval than those during the encoding phase.
source: Using an in vivo multi-fiber photometry system to simultaneously record the Ca2+ activities of both the SuM and DG, we provide the first evidence that activities of the SuM and DG become significantly higher and correlated during spatial memory retrieval than those during the encoding phase (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding supported by data in Figure 1 and illustrated in Figure 7A.

claim: Selective knockdown of SuM glutamate transmission disrupts the correlation of the Ca2+ activities between the SuM and DG during spatial memory retrieval.
source: Importantly, selective knockdown of SuM glutamate transmission disrupts the correlation of the Ca2+ activities between the SuM and DG during spatial memory retrieval (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding supported by data in Figure 6 and illustrated in Figure 7B.

claim: Synchronized SuML-DG activity maybe essential for spatial memory retrieval.
source: Together, these findings suggest that synchronized SuML-DG activity maybe essential for spatial memory retrieval.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the correlation between high SuM-DG synchrony and memory retrieval performance.

claim: The activity of both SuML neurons and SuMLVgat-DG projections are required for spatial memory retrieval.
source: Using circuit-based chemogenetic and optogenetic approaches to specifically manipulate the activity of SuML neurons and SuML-DG projections, we identified that the activity of both SuML neurons and SuMLVgat-DG projections are required for spatial memory retrieval (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding supported by data in Figures 2 and 3 and illustrated in Figure 7C.

claim: SuML glutamate (but not GABA) release from SuML neurons plays a critical role in regulating spatial memory retrieval.
source: Using a genetic approach to selectively knockdown GABA or glutamate release from SuML neurons, we identified that SuML glutamate (but not GABA) release from SuML neurons plays a critical role in regulating spatial memory retrieval (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding supported by data in Figures 4, 5, and 6 and illustrated in Figure 7D.

claim: The combination of high SuML-DG synchrony and high activity in these brain regions maybe required to promote memory retrieval.
source: These results suggest that the combination of high SuML-DG synchrony and high activity in these brain regions maybe required to promote memory retrieval (Frankland et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the observed correlation between high activity/synchrony and memory retrieval, with citation to related work.

claim: SuML and DG activity and correlation may play a relatively minor role in regulating memory encoding.
source: These results suggest that SuML and DG activity and correlation may play a relatively minor role in regulating memory encoding.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the modest changes in activity and correlation during encoding compared to retrieval.

claim: The activity of the SuMLVgat-DG pathway during spatial memory retrieval (but not encoding) is both sufficient and necessary in regulating spatial memory performance during the NPR test.
source: Supporting this, our optogenetic experiments showed that the activity of the SuMLVgat-DG pathway during spatial memory retrieval (but not encoding) is both sufficient and necessary in regulating spatial memory performance during the NPR test.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation based on the optogenetic manipulation experiments in Figure 3.

claim: The cholinergic inputs from the medial septum and diagonal band have been shown to be critical for spatial memory encoding.
source: Indeed, the cholinergic inputs from the medial septum and diagonal band have been shown to be critical for spatial memory encoding (Barry et al., 2012; Hasselmo, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Optogenetic activation of SuML-DG projections excites dentate interneurons (IN).
source: It was recently shown that optogenetic activation of SuML-DG projections excites dentate interneurons (IN), and both monosynaptic and polysynaptic GABAergic inputs have been identified in dentate GCs (Hashimotodani et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent study.

claim: Both monosynaptic and polysynaptic GABAergic inputs have been identified in dentate GCs from SuML.
source: It was recently shown that optogenetic activation of SuML-DG projections excites dentate interneurons (IN), and both monosynaptic and polysynaptic GABAergic inputs have been identified in dentate GCs (Hashimotodani et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent study.

claim: Monosynaptic SuML glutamatergic inputs to GCs play a dominant role in regulating memory retrieval processes.
source: These results suggest that monosynaptic SuML glutamatergic inputs to GCs play a dominant role in regulating memory retrieval processes.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the findings that glutamate (but not GABA) knockdown impairs memory retrieval.

claim: The monosynaptic SuML GABAergic inputs or polysynaptic SuML-IN mediated GABAergic inputs may play a role in regulating long-term memory or other episodic memory processes, such as contextual memory.
source: It is possible that the monosynaptic SuML GABAergic inputs or polysynaptic SuML-IN mediated GABAergic inputs play a role in regulating long-term memory or other episodic memory processes, such as contextual memory.
evidence: This is speculation about potential roles of GABAergic inputs in other memory processes not tested in this study.

claim: Long-range anatomical connections enable multiregional interactions, and such interactions dynamically cope with changing behavioral demands.
source: Accumulating evidence has suggested that long-range anatomical connections enable multiregional interactions, and such interactions dynamically cope with changing behavioral demands (Ito et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to related work.

claim: Neuronal correlation/synchrony has been thought to be critical for behavior-dependent functional coupling of neural circuits through spike-time coordination.
source: Neuronal correlation/synchrony has been thought to be critical for behavior-dependent functional coupling of neural circuits through spike-time coordination (Ito et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to related work.

claim: Ito et al. recorded the local field potentials of SuM and CA1 and found a significant increase of SuM-CA1 coherence in the theta frequency band during the T-maze test.
source: Supporting this view, Ito et al. recorded the local field potentials of SuM and CA1 and found a significant increase of SuM-CA1 coherence in the theta frequency band during the T-maze test, suggesting that the correlation of SuM and CA1 theta rhythm is increased during spatial memory (Ito et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: SuM inputs to DG GCs are weak and not sufficient to drive action potentials in GCs by themselves.
source: A recent study showed that SuM inputs to DG GCs are weak, therefore, they are not sufficient to drive action potentials in GCs by themselves; instead, they can facilitate GC firing elicited by stimulating the perforant pathway (PP) projected from EC (Hashimotodani et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent study.

claim: SuM inputs can facilitate GC firing elicited by stimulating the perforant pathway (PP) projected from EC.
source: A recent study showed that SuM inputs to DG GCs are weak, therefore, they are not sufficient to drive action potentials in GCs by themselves; instead, they can facilitate GC firing elicited by stimulating the perforant pathway (PP) projected from EC (Hashimotodani et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent study.

claim: The SuM can potentially modulate the cortical inputs to the DG and influence DG information processing during the spatial memory process.
source: Therefore, the SuM can potentially modulate the cortical inputs to the DG and influence DG information processing during the spatial memory process.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known modulatory role of SuM inputs on PP-GC synapses.

claim: The high SuM-DG synchrony may play a critical role in ensuring the spike-timing precision of the modulatory action of the SuM on PP-GC synapses during the spatial memory process.
source: The high SuM-DG synchrony may play a critical role in ensuring the spike-timing precision of the modulatory action of the SuM on PP-GC synapses during the spatial memory process.
evidence: This is speculation about the functional significance of SuM-DG synchrony.

claim: Aberrant neuronal synchronization is associated with Alzheimer's disease, which may in part contribute to the cognitive deficits seen in this disease.
source: Ample studies have shown that aberrant neuronal synchronization is associated with Alzheimer's disease, which may in part contribute to the cognitive deficits seen in this disease (Palop and Mucke, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: EC and hippocampus are impaired during early AD.
source: It has been well established that EC and hippocampus are impaired during early AD (Harris et al., 2010; Hyman et al., 1986), therefore, our findings may guide novel therapeutic strategies to treat AD-associated memory deficits by targeting SuM inputs to enhance SuM-DG synchrony and modulate EC inputs onto GCs.
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.
